label: thm:LuoSun
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: Recently, Cui and Sun \cite{CuiSun} obtained a topological sphere theorem for Legendrian submanifolds in the unit sphere under the same pinching condition as in Theorem \ref{thm:LuoSun}.
head: environment

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
Let $F:M^n\to\mathbb S^{2n+1}\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ be a minimal Legendrian
immersion of a connected closed manifold, $n\ge3$. If $|B|^2\lec_n$
everywhere, then, up to a unitary transformation, $F$ parametrizes a
totally geodesic sphere or is a finite covering of the embedded image
\begin{equation}\tag{1.1}\label{eq:1.1}
 (\theta,x)\longmapsto
 \left(\frac{e^{in\theta}}{\sqrt{n+1}},
       \sqrt{\frac n{n+1}}e^{-i\theta}x\right),
 \qquad(\theta,x)\in\mathbb S^1\times\mathbb S^{n-1}.
\end{equation}
Here $\mathbb S^1=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$. For odd $n$ the displayed map is
an embedding; for even $n$ it induces an embedding on the quotient by
$(\theta,x)\sim(\theta+\pi,-x)$.
head: environment

label: lem:gram
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:gram}
Every trace-free symmetric cubic on $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge3$, satisfies
$0\le G\le\alpha Sg$. If $S>0$ and $G(e,e)=\alpha S$ for a unit vector
$e=e_1$, then
\[
 \sigma_{111}=a,\qquad \sigma_{1\beta\gamma}=-\frac{a}{n-1}\delta_{\beta\gamma},
 \qquad \sigma_{11\beta}=\sigma_{\beta\gamma\delta}=0,\qquad
 S=\frac{n+2}{n-1}a^2,
\]
where Greek indices are greater than one. In this equality case, the largest
Gram eigenvalue is simple. In particular, $S\le c_n$ implies
$\operatorname{Ric}\ge0$.

title: Proof

label: lem:derivative
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:derivative}
For $t\ge\tau_n$, one has $\mathcal D_t\ge0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $T_{ijkl}=\sigma_{ijk;l}$, and set, within this proof,
\[
 E_{ijk}=\sigma_{iab}T_{abjk},\qquad
 \Gamma_i=\sigma_{abc}T_{abci},\qquad
 E^s_{ijk}=(E_{ijk}+E_{jik}+E_{kij})/3.
\]
The last two indices of $E$ are symmetric, and trace-freeness gives
$\sum_j E_{ijj}=0$ and $\sum_j E_{jij}=\Gamma_i$.
Differentiation of $G$ and expansion of the three summands in $E^s$ yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \nabla_iG_{jk}&=E_{jik}+E_{kij},\\
 \nabla_iG_{jk}\nabla_jG_{ik}&=|E|^2+3E_{ijk}E_{jik},\\
 |E^s|^2&=\tfrac13\bigl(|E|^2+2E_{ijk}E_{jik}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \nabla_iG_{jk}\nabla_jG_{ik}=-\tfrac12|E|^2+\tfrac92|E^s|^2,
 \qquad \operatorname{tr}E^s=\tfrac23\Gamma.
\]
For $(\delta\Gamma)_{ijk}=\delta_{ij}\Gamma_k+\delta_{ik}\Gamma_j
+\delta_{jk}\Gamma_i$,
\[
 |\delta\Gamma|^2=3(n+2)|\Gamma|^2,\qquad
 |E^s|^2=\left|E^s-\frac{2}{3(n+2)}\delta\Gamma\right|^2
             +\frac{4}{3(n+2)}|\Gamma|^2.
\]
Using $\nabla S=2\Gamma$ yields
\[
 \mathcal D_{\tau_n}
 =\tfrac12\bigl(\alpha S|T|^2-|E|^2\bigr)
  +\tfrac92\left|E^s-\frac{2}{3(n+2)}\delta\Gamma\right|^2
  +\frac{4}{n+2}|\Gamma|^2.
\]
Order the Gram eigenvalues as $g_1\ge\cdots\ge g_n\ge0$.
In a corresponding orthonormal eigenframe, the matrices $A_i/\sqrt{g_i}$
with $g_i>0$ are orthonormal; if $g_i=0$, then $A_i=0$.
For a symmetric matrix $U$, Bessel's inequality gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sum_i\langle A_i,U\rangle^2
 &=\sum_{g_i>0}g_i\left\langle\frac{A_i}{\sqrt{g_i}},U\right\rangle^2\\
 &\le g_1\sum_{g_i>0}\left\langle\frac{A_i}{\sqrt{g_i}},U\right\rangle^2
 \le g_1|U|^2\le\alpha S|U|^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Apply this to $U_{ab}=T_{abjk}$ and sum over $j,k$ to obtain
$|E|^2\le\alpha S|T|^2$. Finally,
\[
 \mathcal D_t-\mathcal D_{\tau_n}=(t-\tau_n)\left(S|T|^2+\tfrac12|\nabla S|^2\right)\ge0.
\]

label: lem:projection
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:3.5
title: Proof
body_md:
To estimate $Q$, take the completely symmetric part of the contracted product
$\sigma_{ija}\sigma_{kla}$:
\[
 \mathcal A_{ijkl}
 =\frac13(\sigma_{ija}\sigma_{kla}+\sigma_{ika}\sigma_{jla}
       +\sigma_{ila}\sigma_{jka}),\qquad K=h_4\mathcal A.
\]
The metric insertions are
\begin{align*}
 (\delta G)_{ijkl}
 &=\delta_{ij}G_{kl}+\delta_{ik}G_{jl}+\delta_{il}G_{jk}
   +\delta_{jk}G_{il}+\delta_{jl}G_{ik}+\delta_{kl}G_{ij},\\
 (\delta\delta)_{ijkl}
 &=\delta_{ij}\delta_{kl}+\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}
   +\delta_{il}\delta_{jk}.
\end{align*}
For a symmetric two-tensor $H$ and a symmetric four-tensor $U$, complete
symmetry gives
\[
 \langle\delta H,U\rangle=6\langle H,\operatorname{tr}U\rangle,
 \qquad
 \langle\delta\delta,U\rangle=3\operatorname{tr}^2U,
\]
where $\operatorname{tr}^2U=\sum_{i,j}U_{iijj}$. Thus the metric insertions
are orthogonal to trace-free symmetric four-tensors. Taking traces gives
\[
 \operatorname{tr}\mathcal A=\frac23G,\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}(\delta G)=(n+4)G+g,\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}(\delta\delta)=(n+2)g.
\]
It follows that the orthogonal trace part is
\[
 \mathcal A-K=\frac{2}{3(n+4)}\delta G
 -\frac{2}{3(n+4)(n+2)}\delta\delta.
\]
Its squared norm can be computed by pairing once with $\mathcal A$:
\[
 |\mathcal A-K|^2
 =\langle\mathcal A,\mathcal A-K\rangle
 =\frac{8}{3(n+4)}p_2-\frac{4}{3(n+2)(n+4)}.
\]
If $H_0=\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{tr}(A_iA_jA_iA_j)$, then
$Q=3p_2-2H_0$ and $|\mathcal A|^2=(p_2+2H_0)/3$. The first identity
follows from $\sum_iA_i^2=G$; the second follows by expanding the three
squared terms and six cross terms in $|\mathcal A|^2$. Subtracting the trace
part yields
\begin{equation}\tag{3.5}\label{eq:3.5}
 3|K|^2=\frac{4(n+2)}{n+4}p_2
       +\frac{4}{(n+2)(n+4)}-Q,
 \qquad K_{iabc}\sigma_{abc}=\frac{n+2}{n+4}V_i.
\end{equation}
For the second identity, first note that
$\mathcal A_{iabc}\sigma_{abc}=V_i$. In $\delta G$, exactly three metric
insertions survive the contraction, each contributing $V_i$.

For a unit vector $e$, put $A_e=\sigma(e,\cdot,\cdot)$ and
$T_e=\operatorname{Sym}(e^\flat\otimes\sigma)$, where the four placements
are averaged. The four diagonal terms and twelve cross terms in $|T_e|^2$
give
\[
 |T_e|^2=\frac14+\frac34|A_e|^2,\qquad
 \operatorname{tr}T_e=\frac12A_e,\qquad
 h_4T_e=T_e-\frac{\delta A_e}{2(n+4)}.
\]
The same trace pairing then gives
\begin{align*}
 |h_4T_e|^2
 &=|T_e|^2-\frac{\langle\delta A_e,T_e\rangle}{2(n+4)}\\
 &=\frac14+\frac34|A_e|^2-\frac{3|A_e|^2}{2(n+4)}
 =\frac14+\frac{3(n+2)}{4(n+4)}G(e,e).
\end{align*}
When $V\ne0$, choose $e=V^\sharp/|V|$. Since
$\langle K,h_4T_e\rangle=(n+2)|V|/(n+4)$ and $G(e,e)\le\ell$,
Cauchy's inequality gives
\[
 \frac{(n+2)^2}{(n+4)^2}r
 =\langle K,h_4T_e\rangle^2
 \le |K|^2\left\{\frac14+\frac{3(n+2)}{4(n+4)}\ell\right\}.
\]
Eliminating $|K|^2$ by \eqref{eq:3.5} yields
\begin{equation}\tag{3.6}\label{eq:3.6}
 Q\le\frac{4(n+2)}{n+4}p_2
     +\frac{4}{(n+2)(n+4)}-k(\ell)r.
\end{equation}
For $V=0$ this follows from $|K|^2\ge0$.

Next, $\operatorname{tr}N=2V$ and $\langle N,\sigma\rangle=3p_2$ imply
\begin{equation}\tag{3.7}\label{eq:3.7}
 |N|^2=9p_2^2+\frac{12}{n+2}r+|W|^2.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the trace part of $N$ is $2\delta V/(n+2)$, with squared norm
$12r/(n+2)$, and $W\perp\sigma$. In a Gram eigenframe,
\[
 |N|^2=3p_3+6\sum_{i,j,a}g_ig_j\sigma_{ija}^2,
 \qquad
 \frac12\sum_a|[G,A_a]|^2
 =p_3-\sum_{i,j,a}g_ig_j\sigma_{ija}^2.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:2.6} becomes
\[
 \mathcal B_\tau=\frac{n}{c_n}p_2+\frac{\tau(n+1)-1}{c_n}
 -\tau Q-\frac32p_3+\frac16|N|^2-r.
\]
Substituting \eqref{eq:3.6} and \eqref{eq:3.7} gives \eqref{eq:3.3}; the
coefficient of $r$ is $\tau k(\ell)+2/(n+2)-1=z(\ell)$. Also $k$ is
decreasing and
\begin{equation}\tag{3.8}\label{eq:3.8}
 z(\ell)\ge z(\alpha)
 =\frac{n(n^2+2n+4)}{2(n+1)(n+2)(n+4)}>0.
\end{equation}

To bound $r$ from below, split the cubic relative to a largest-eigenvalue
direction. The quantity $2\ell-1$ arising in this split is positive precisely
in the range now under consideration, $\ell>1/2$. Choose a Gram eigenframe
with $g_1=\ell$ and put
\begin{gather*}
 m=n-1,\qquad \mu=\frac{1-\ell}{m},\qquad d=\ell-\mu,\\
 Z=G|_{e_1^\perp}-\mu I,\qquad \eta=|Z|^2,\qquad
 \mathcal K=\frac{m}{m-1}d^2-\eta=L-p_2.
\end{gather*}
Since $p_2\le\ell^2+(1-\ell)^2$,
\[
 \mathcal K\ge(2\ell-1)
 \left(1+\frac{2\ell-1}{n-2}\right)>0.
\]
Let $a_i=\sigma_{i11}$ and
$T_{i\beta\gamma}=\sigma_{i\beta\gamma}+a_i\delta_{\beta\gamma}/m$.
Each $T_i$ is trace-free on the transverse indices. Here
$|a_\bullet|^2=\sum_i a_i^2$ and
$|T|^2=\sum_{i,\beta,\gamma}T_{i\beta\gamma}^2$. Separating the entries
according to the number of indices equal to $1$ gives
\[
 S=2\ell-|a_\bullet|^2+\sum_{i,\beta,\gamma}\sigma_{i\beta\gamma}^2,
 \qquad
 |T|^2=\sum_{i,\beta,\gamma}\sigma_{i\beta\gamma}^2
       -\frac{|a_\bullet|^2}{m}.
\]
Since $S=1$ and $G$ is diagonal in the chosen frame, it follows that
\[
 2\ell-1=\frac{m-1}{m}|a_\bullet|^2-|T|^2,
 \qquad V_i=da_i+\langle T_i,Z\rangle.
\]
With $\rho=(m-1)/(md)$, the required square completion is
\[
 r-(2\ell-1)\mathcal K
 =\mathcal K\sum_i|T_i+\rho a_iZ|^2
  +\sum_i\langle T_i+\rho a_iZ,Z\rangle^2\ge0.
\]
Expanding the right-hand side,
$\mathcal K+\eta=md^2/(m-1)$ gives the cross coefficient
$2\rho(\mathcal K+\eta)=2d$ and the $|a_\bullet|^2$ coefficient
$\rho^2\eta(\mathcal K+\eta)=(m-1)\eta/m$.
Together with \eqref{eq:3.8}, this proves \eqref{eq:3.4}.
head: environment

label: prop:lower
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:lower}
For $n\ge4$ and $\ell\le1/2$, one has $\mathcal B_\tau>0$.
head: environment

label: eq:3.9
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $p_2=\sum_i g_i^2\le\frac12\sum_i g_i=1/2$, set
$x=1/2-p_2\ge0$. For every real $a$,
\[
 0\le\sum_i(1/2-g_i)(g_i-a)^2
 =\frac12p_2-p_3-2ax+\frac{n-2}{2}a^2.
\]
Taking $a=2x/(n-2)$ yields $p_3\le p_2/2-2x^2/(n-2)$. After discarding
the nonnegative $r$ and $W$ terms in \eqref{eq:3.3}, we obtain
\begin{gather*}
 \mathcal B_\tau\ge D_n-L_nx+\frac{3n}{2(n-2)}x^2,\\
 D_n=\frac A2+C
 =\frac{n(n-2)(3n+2)}{2(n-1)(n+2)^2(n+4)},\qquad
 L_n=A+\frac34.
\end{gather*}
Division in the dimension parameter gives
\begin{equation}\tag{3.9}\label{eq:3.9}
 A=-1+\frac7{n+4}+\frac{6-n}{(n-1)(n+2)(n+4)}.
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
 \frac3n-L_n
 &=\frac1{n+4}\left\{
 \frac{(n-6)^2+12}{4n}+\frac{n-6}{(n-1)(n+2)}\right\}\\
 &\ge\frac1{n+4}\left\{\frac3n-\frac2{(n-1)(n+2)}\right\}>0.
\end{align*}
Here $n\ge4$ and $(n-1)(n+2)>n$. The constant term satisfies
\begin{equation}\tag{3.10}\label{eq:3.10}
 D_n-\frac{3(n-2)}{4n(n+2)}
 =\frac{(n-2)\{(n-4)(3n^2+n-2)+16\}}
        {4n(n-1)(n+2)^2(n+4)}>0.
\end{equation}
Using $x\ge0$ before replacing the linear coefficient, we get
\[
 \mathcal B_\tau>
 \frac{3n}{2(n-2)}\left(x-\frac{n-2}{n^2}\right)^2
 +\frac{3(n-2)(n^2-2n-4)}{4n^3(n+2)}>0.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:interpolation
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:4.6
title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\varepsilon=\alpha-\ell$, $d=(n\ell-1)/(n-1)$ and $\Lambda=n+4+3(n+2)\ell$. The identities
\[
 \bar p_2=\frac{1+(n-1)d^2}{n},\qquad
 \bar p_2^2-\bar p_3=-\ell(1-\ell)d^2,\qquad
 L-\bar p_2=\frac{n-1}{n-2}d^2
\]
reduce \eqref{eq:4.3} to
\begin{equation}
 b_0=\frac An+C+d^2\left\{
       \frac{n-1}{n}A-\frac32\ell(1-\ell)
       +\frac{n-1}{n-2}(2\ell-1)z(\ell)\right\}.
 \tag{4.6}\label{eq:4.6}
\end{equation}
In particular, $b_0(\alpha)=0$. For $\ell<\alpha$, define $\varphi_n(\ell)=b_0(\ell)/(\alpha-\ell)$. The following computation also establishes its continuous extension at $\alpha$. Write
\[
 d_0=\frac{(n-2)(n+1)}{(n-1)(n+2)},\qquad
 c=\frac{3n(n-1)(n+2)(5n+14)}{8(n-2)(n+1)^2(n+4)},\qquad
 D=\frac{\Lambda}{4(n+1)}.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 \varphi_n={}&\frac{n(n-2)}{2(n-1)(n+2)}
  +\frac{n}{2(n+1)}d
  +\left(2+\frac1{n-2}-\frac3{2n}\right)d^2\\
 &-\frac{3(n-1)}{2n}d^3-\frac{cd^2}{D}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.7}\label{eq:4.7}
\end{equation}
To obtain this expression, evaluate the constant term and the coefficient of $d^2$ in \eqref{eq:4.6} at $\ell=\alpha$:
\[
 \frac An+C=\frac{(n-2)^2(n+1)}{2(n-1)(n+2)^2},
\]
\[
 \left\{\frac{n-1}{n}A-\frac32\ell(1-\ell)
 +\frac{n-1}{n-2}(2\ell-1)z(\ell)\right\}_{\ell=\alpha}
 =-\frac{n-1}{2(n+1)}.
\]
These values satisfy $b_0(\alpha)=0$ and $d_0-d=n\varepsilon/(n-1)$. The only rational subtraction is
\[
 \frac{(2\ell-1)z(\ell)-(2\alpha-1)z(\alpha)}{\varepsilon}
 =2\alpha-\frac{3n(n+2)(5n+14)}{2(n+1)(n+4)\Lambda}.
\]
Indeed, in the two linear fractions defining $z$, the denominator at $\alpha$ is $4(n+1)$ and the cross-multiplied numerator is linear in $\ell-\alpha$. Subtracting $b_0(\alpha)$ from \eqref{eq:4.6} now gives
\[
 \varphi_n=\frac{n}{2(n+1)}(d_0+d)
 +d^2\left\{-\frac32(2\alpha-1)+\frac32\varepsilon
 +\frac{2\alpha(n-1)}{n-2}-\frac cD\right\}.
\]
Substitute $\varepsilon=(n-1)(d_0-d)/n$ to obtain \eqref{eq:4.7}.

We compare $\varphi_n$ with its affine endpoint interpolant. Put
\[
 a=\frac{n+6}{4n},\qquad
 h=\frac{3(n-1)(n+2)}{4n(n+1)},\qquad
 D(d)=a+hd.
\]
Here $a,h,c$ are positive. Regard \eqref{eq:4.7} as the function $\Phi(d)=\varphi_n((1+(n-1)d)/n)$. For $u<v$, let
\[
 (\mathcal Lf)(d)=\frac{v-d}{v-u}f(u)+\frac{d-u}{v-u}f(v)
\]
be the affine interpolant at $u,v$. The three elementary differences needed for \eqref{eq:4.7} are
\begin{align*}
 d^2-\mathcal L(d^2)&=-(d-u)(v-d),\\
 d^3-\mathcal L(d^3)&=-(d-u)(v-d)(d+u+v),\\
 \frac{d^2}{D(d)}-\mathcal L\left(\frac{d^2}{D(d)}\right)
 &=-\frac{a^2(d-u)(v-d)}{D(d)D(u)D(v)}.
\end{align*}
For the last identity, divide $d^2/D(d)=d/h-a/h^2+a^2/(h^2D(d))$; the affine terms cancel, and direct subtraction of the remaining three reciprocals gives the displayed expression. Since the constant and linear terms in \eqref{eq:4.7} also cancel, we have the exact remainder formula
\begin{equation}
 \Phi(d)-\mathcal L\Phi(d)=(d-u)(v-d)H_{u,v}(d),
 \tag{4.8}\label{eq:4.8}
\end{equation}
where
\[
 H_{u,v}(d)=-2-\frac1{n-2}+\frac3{2n}
 +\frac{3(n-1)}{2n}(d+u+v)+\frac{ca^2}{D(d)D(u)D(v)}.
\]
On $u\le d\le v$, use only $d\ge u$ and $D(d)\le D(v)$:
\begin{equation}
 H_{u,v}(d)\ge-2-\frac1{n-2}+\frac3{2n}
 +\frac{3(n-1)}{2n}(2u+v)+\frac{ca^2}{D(u)D(v)^2}
 =:H_*.
 \tag{4.9}\label{eq:4.9}
\end{equation}
Choose $u=(n-2)/(2(n-1))$, corresponding to $\ell=1/2$. For $n=4,5,6$ take $v=d_0$, corresponding to $\ell=\alpha$. Here
\[
 D(u)=\frac{5n+14}{8(n+1)},\qquad D(v)=1,
\]
\[
 H_*=\frac{n^3-7n^2+12}{n(n-2)(n+2)}
 +\frac{3(n-1)(n+2)(n+6)^2}{16n(n-2)(n+1)(n+4)}.
\]
Substitution gives the positive values
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
 n&4&5&6\\\hline
 H_*&39/128&3193/7560&29/56
 \end{array}.
\]
For $n\ge7$ take $v=(2n-3)/(3(n-1))$, corresponding to $\ell=2/3$. Then $D(v)=(3n+8)/(4(n+1))$, and cancellation in \eqref{eq:4.9} gives
\[
 H_*=\frac12-\frac3n-\frac1{n-2}
 +3\frac{(n^2-1)(n+2)}{n(n-2)(n+4)}
 \left(\frac{n+6}{3n+8}\right)^2.
\]
The first fraction in the last term is greater than one, because
\[
 (n^2-1)(n+2)-n(n-2)(n+4)=7n-2>0;
\]
the squared fraction is greater than $1/9$. Consequently,
\[
 H_*>\frac12-\frac12-\frac14+\frac13=\frac1{12}>0.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:4.8} puts $\Phi$ above its endpoint interpolant on each required interval.

It remains to check the endpoints against $(1-\ell)/2$, which is affine in $d$. At $\ell=1/2$, substitution of $d=(n-2)/(2(n-1))$ and $\Lambda=(5n+14)/2$ into \eqref{eq:4.7} gives
\begin{equation}
 \varphi_n(1/2)-\frac14
 =\frac{(n-4)(n^3+18n^2-8n-16)}{16(n-1)^2(n+2)(n+4)}\ge0.
 \tag{4.10}\label{eq:4.10}
\end{equation}
For $n=4,5,6$, use $d=d_0$ and $D(d_0)=1$ in the same formula:
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
 n&4&5&6\\\hline
 \varphi_n(\alpha)-1/(n+2)&7/216&481/10976&29/800
 \end{array}.
\]
For $n\ge7$, the right endpoint is $2/3$. Substituting $d=(2n-3)/(3(n-1))$ and $\Lambda=3n+8$ gives
\[
 \varphi_n(2/3)-\frac16
 =\frac{2\{n(n-4)(16n^2+37n-3)+6(27n+32)\}}
 {9(n-2)(n-1)(n+2)(n+4)(3n+8)}>0.
\]
The endpoint interpolation now yields $\varphi_n(\ell)\ge(1-\ell)/2$ throughout the required intervals. Multiplication by $\alpha-\ell\ge0$ proves the lemma, including the Calabi endpoint by continuous extension.
head: environment

label: lem:opposite
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:4.12
title: Proof
body_md:
At $\eta=q$, the two moments in \eqref{eq:4.2} are $\ell^2+(1-\ell)^2$ and $\ell^3+(1-\ell)^3$. Put $x=2\ell-1\in[0,1/3]$ and $v=1/3$. Using $\ell(1-\ell)=(1-x^2)/4$ gives
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
 b_2&=D_n+x^2\omega(x),\\
 \omega(x)&=\frac38x^2+\frac A2-\frac38
 +z((1+x)/2)\left(1+\frac{x}{n-2}\right),
\end{aligned}
\tag{4.12}\label{eq:4.12}
\end{equation}
where $D_n=A/2+C>0$ is the constant in \eqref{eq:3.10}. To estimate $\omega$, set
\[
 a_* =\frac{5n+14}{3(n+2)},\qquad b_* =\frac{4n}{n+4}.
\]
Then $z((1+x)/2)=b_* /(a_*+x)-\alpha$, and
\[
 n-2-a_* =\frac{(n-4)(3n+7)+2}{3(n+2)}>0.
\]
Subtract the two quadratic terms and the two linear fractions in \eqref{eq:4.12}. This gives directly
\[
 \omega(x)-\omega(v)
 =(v-x)\left\{-\frac38(x+v)
 +\frac{b_*(1-a_* /(n-2))}{(a_*+x)(a_*+v)}
 +\frac{\alpha}{n-2}\right\}.
\]
Since $x\le v$, the braces are bounded below by
\[
 -\frac14+\frac{b_*}{(a_*+v)^2}
 \left(1-\frac{a_*}{n-2}\right)+\frac{\alpha}{n-2}.
\]
The factor in parentheses is positive, and
\[
 \frac{b_*}{(a_*+v)^2}
 =\frac{n}{n+4}\left(1-\frac2{3n+8}\right)^2
 \ge\frac12(9/10)^2>\frac25.
\]
Also $a_*\le17/9$ and $\alpha\ge2/3$, so the braces exceed
\[
 -\frac14+\frac25-\frac4{45(n-2)}
 \ge-\frac14+\frac25-\frac2{45}>0.
\]
Hence $\omega(x)\ge\omega(1/3)$.

To check the resulting endpoint, set $z_2=z(2/3)>0$. Substitution of $x=1/3$ into \eqref{eq:4.12} gives
\begin{equation}
 E_n:=b_2(2/3)-\frac1{54}
 =D_n+\frac A{18}-\frac1{18}+\frac{3n-5}{27(n-2)}z_2.
 \tag{4.13}\label{eq:4.13}
\end{equation}
For $n=4$, the values $D_4=7/108$, $A=-1/9$ and $z_2=7/30$ give $E_4=1/30>0$. For $n\ge5$, discard the following explicitly positive differences:
\begin{align*}
 A-\left(-1+\frac6{n+4}\right)
 &=\frac{n^2+4}{(n-1)(n+2)(n+4)}>0,\\
 z_2-\left(1-\frac8{n+4}\right)
 &=\frac{2(n^2+16n+32)}{(n+2)(n+4)(3n+8)}>0,\\
 \frac{3n-5}{27(n-2)}-\frac19
 &=\frac1{27(n-2)}>0.
\end{align*}
Use the last estimate first, with $z_2>0$, and then the first two in \eqref{eq:4.13}. The constant terms cancel, leaving
\[
\begin{aligned}
 E_n&>D_n-\frac5{9(n+4)}
 >\frac{3(n-2)}{4n(n+2)}-\frac5{9(n+4)}\\
 &=\frac{(n-5)(7n+49)+29}{36n(n+2)(n+4)}>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the second inequality is \eqref{eq:3.10}. Finally, the expression $D_n+x^2\{\omega(1/3)-1/6\}$ is affine in $x^2\in[0,1/9]$. Therefore
\[
 b_2-x^2/6\ge D_n+x^2\{\omega(1/3)-1/6\}
 \ge\min\{D_n,E_n\}>0,
\]
as required.
head: environment

label: prop:middle
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:middle}
For $n\ge4$ and $1/2\le\ell\le2/3$, one has $\mathcal B_\tau\ge0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:4.4}, it remains to verify the signs of $b_0,b_1,b_2$. Lemmas \ref{lem:interpolation} and \ref{lem:opposite} give $b_0\ge0$ and $b_2>0$. To bound $b_1$, put $x=2\ell-1$ and $\rho=2\alpha-1=(n-2)/(n+2)$. Then
\[
 \alpha-\ell=(\rho-x)/2,\qquad 1-\ell=(1-x)/2,\qquad
 q=\frac{\rho}{1+3\rho}(1-x)^2,\qquad \rho\ge1/3.
\]
The inequality
\[
 \frac\rho{12}-\frac{\rho^2}{(1+3\rho)^2}
 =\frac{\rho(3\rho-1)^2}{12(1+3\rho)^2}\ge0
\]
together with \eqref{eq:4.5} and \eqref{eq:4.11} gives
\begin{align*}
 2b_1&>\frac{(\rho-x)(1-x)}8+\frac{x^2}6
 -\frac{3\rho^2}{2(1+3\rho)^2}(1-x)^4\\
 &\ge\frac{3(\rho-x)(1-x)+4x^2-3\rho(1-x)^4}{24}\\
 &=\frac{3(\rho-1/3)x(1-x)(3-3x+x^2)+x^2(1+4x-x^2)}{24}\ge0.
\end{align*}
The quadratic is nonnegative on its required interval.
head: environment

label: prop:small-upper
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:small-upper}
For $n=5,6$ and $2/3\le\ell\le\alpha$, one has $\mathcal B_\tau\ge0$.
head: environment

label: eq:4.14
title: Proof
head: environment

label: lem:gap
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a Gram eigenframe with $g_1=\ell$, and put $E=e_1\otimes e_1$.
Let $Z_1$ be the unit trace-free symmetric cubic with independent components
\[
 (Z_1)_{111}=\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n+2}},\qquad
 (Z_1)_{1\beta\gamma}=-\frac{\delta_{\beta\gamma}}{\sqrt{(n-1)(n+2)}},
 \qquad (Z_1)_{11\beta}=(Z_1)_{\beta\gamma\delta}=0.
\]
Its Rayleigh quotient is
\[
 \langle T_GZ_1,Z_1\rangle
 =\alpha\ell+\frac{2}{(n-1)(n+2)}\sum_{i>1}g_i=a.
\]
Hence the largest eigenvalue of $T_G$ is at least $a$.

For $U\perp Z_1$, the axial scalar component in the decomposition
\eqref{eq:2.1} vanishes. Therefore
\[
 \langle T_EU,U\rangle=2|u|^2+|C|^2
 \le\frac{2(n+1)}{3(n+2)}|U|^2.
\]
Since the transverse Gram eigenvalues have sum $1-\ell$,
\[
 G\le(1-\ell)I+(2\ell-1)E.
\]
The order property gives $\langle T_GU,U\rangle\le b|U|^2$ on the
codimension-one space $Z_1^\perp$. By the min--max principle, the second
and all subsequent eigenvalues of $T_G$ are at most $b$. Finally,
\[
 a-b=\frac{(n-2)\{2(n+2)\ell-n-5\}}{3(n-1)(n+2)}\ge0.
\]
Thus the spectrum avoids $(b,a)$, including the case $a=b$, and
$(T_G-aI)(T_G-bI)\ge0$. Pairing with $\sigma$ and using
\eqref{eq:5.1} yields
\[
 |T_G\sigma|^2-(a+b)p_2+ab\ge0,
 \qquad \frac{|W|^2}{9}=|T_G\sigma|^2-p_2^2,
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:5.3}. At the Calabi cubic, $T_G\sigma=p_2\sigma$ and $a=p_2$, so equality
holds in \eqref{eq:5.3}.
head: environment

label: prop:upper
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:5.4
title: Proof
body_md:
The spectral-gap hypothesis holds because
\[
 \frac23-\frac{n+5}{2(n+2)}=\frac{n-7}{6(n+2)}\ge0.
\]
Use the transverse moments and $\eta$ from Section~\ref{sec:intermediate}.
Substitution of \eqref{eq:5.3} into \eqref{eq:3.4} cancels the quadratic
moment:
\[
 \frac32p_2^2+\frac16|W|^2
 \ge\frac32(a+b)p_2-\frac32ab.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:4.1}, this gives the affine bound
\begin{equation}
 \mathcal B_{\tau_n}\ge F_n(\ell)+M_n(\ell)\eta,
 \tag{5.4}\label{eq:5.4}
\end{equation}
where
\[
 F_n=b_0+\frac32(a-\bar p_2)(\bar p_2-b),
 \qquad
 M_n=A-(2\ell-1)z+\frac32(a+b)-\frac{3n}{2(n-1)}(1-\ell).
\]
We estimate the two coefficients separately.

By \eqref{eq:4.14}, $z<1$ and $z'<0$ for $\ell\ge2/3$.
Differentiating \eqref{eq:5.2} gives
\[
 M_n'=-2z-(2\ell-1)z'
       +\frac32\left(a'+b'+\frac{n}{n-1}\right)
 >\frac{3n^2-4n+4}{2(n-1)(n+2)}>0.
\]
At the left endpoint, use $z(2/3)<1$ before combining the fractions:
\[
 \begin{split}
 M_n(2/3)
 &>A-\frac13+\frac32\{a(2/3)+b(2/3)\}-\frac{n}{2(n-1)}\\
 &=\frac{25n^2-18n+8}{6(n-1)(n+2)(n+4)}>0.
 \end{split}
\]
Thus $M_n>0$ throughout the interval.

Set $\varepsilon=\alpha-\ell$ and $d=(n\ell-1)/(n-1)$.
The identity $a-\bar p_2=d\varepsilon$ gives
\[
 \frac{F_n}{\varepsilon}=\varphi_n+\frac32d(\bar p_2-b)
 \qquad(\varepsilon>0).
\]
Use \eqref{eq:4.7} and $\bar p_2=(1+(n-1)d^2)/n$.
The cubic terms cancel, and retaining the linear denominator gives
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 \frac{F_n}{\varepsilon}
 &=\frac{n(n-2)}{2(n-1)(n+2)}
   -\frac{n^2-6n-8}{2n(n+1)(n+2)}d\\
 &\quad+\left\{
 \frac{3n^3+4n^2-20n+16}{2n(n-2)(n+2)}
 -\frac{3n(n-1)(n+2)(5n+14)}{2(n-2)(n+1)(n+4)\Lambda}
 \right\}d^2.
 \end{split}
 \tag{5.5}\label{eq:5.5}
\end{equation}
All terms extend continuously to $\varepsilon=0$.

Multiply \eqref{eq:5.5} by the positive denominator
\[
 n\Lambda=(n+1)(n+6)+3(n-1)(n+2)d,
\]
and put $P(d)=n\Lambda F_n/\varepsilon$.
The rational subtraction contributes only
\[
 -\frac{3n^2(n-1)(n+2)(5n+14)}{2(n-2)(n+1)(n+4)}d^2.
\]
Multiplying the other coefficients by the two terms of $n\Lambda$ and
collecting equal powers of $d$ gives
\begin{equation}
 \begin{split}
 P(d)
 &=\frac{n^2}{2}\{1-d+d(3d-2)^2\}
   +\frac n2(4-7d+10d^2+21d^3)\\
 &\quad-5+d-2d^2-15d^3
   +\frac{4(4+6d-9d^2)}{3(n+2)}-\frac7{3(n-1)}\\
 &\quad+\frac{4d^2(3d-2)}{n-2}
   +\frac{12d(1-d)^2}{n}+\frac{80d^2}{n+4}.
 \end{split}
 \tag{5.6}\label{eq:5.6}
\end{equation}
On the actual spectral range,
\[
 \frac12\le\frac{2n-3}{3(n-1)}\le d
 \le\frac{(n-2)(n+1)}{(n-1)(n+2)}<1.
\]
It suffices to estimate \eqref{eq:5.6} on $1/2\le d\le1$.
Write
\[
 H_0(d)=1-d+d(3d-2)^2,\quad
 Q_0(d)=4-7d+10d^2+21d^3,\quad
 C_0(d)=-5+d-2d^2-15d^3,
\]
and denote the five fractions in \eqref{eq:5.6} by $R_n(d)$.
Here $H_0\ge0$ and, since $d^2\ge d/2$,
\[
 Q_0\ge4-2d+21d^3>0.
\]
Also $4+6d-9d^2\ge4-3d\ge1$. Only two terms of $R_n$ can be
negative, and
\[
 -\frac7{3(n-1)}> -\frac12,
 \qquad
 \frac{4d^2(3d-2)}{n-2}\ge-\frac2{n-2}\ge-\frac12.
\]
Hence $R_n>-1$. Put $x=d-1/2\ge0$. As $n/2\ge3$,
\[
 \begin{split}
 P(d)&>\frac{n^2}{2}H_0(d)+3Q_0(d)+C_0(d)-1\\
 &=\frac{n^2}{2}H_0(d)+9+44x+100x^2+48x^3\ge9.
 \end{split}
\]
Consequently,
\[
 F_n(\ell)>\frac{9(\alpha-\ell)}{n\Lambda}>0
 \qquad(\ell<\alpha).
\]
The quotient in \eqref{eq:5.5} has a finite limit at $\ell=\alpha$,
so $F_n(\alpha)=0$. Since $\Lambda\le4(n+1)\le6n$,
$9/(n\Lambda)\ge1/n^2$.
The lower bound for $M_n(2/3)$ holds throughout the interval and is
larger than $1/n$: indeed, for $n\ge7$,
\[
 25n^2-18n+8>18n^2,
 \qquad
 6(n-1)(n+2)(n+4)<6n\cdot\frac{3n}{2}\cdot2n=18n^3.
\]
Discarding the excess in both coefficients therefore gives
\[
 \mathcal B_{\tau_n}\ge\frac{\alpha-\ell}{n^2}+\frac\eta n\ge0.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $S=0$ the assertion is immediate. If $n\ge4$, normalize $S=1$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:lower} covers $\ell\le1/2$ and
Proposition~\ref{prop:middle} covers $1/2\le\ell\le2/3$.
For $n=4$, $\alpha=2/3$, so there is no further interval.
For $n=5,6$, Proposition~\ref{prop:small-upper} covers $[2/3,\alpha]$;
for $n\ge7$, this interval is covered by Proposition~\ref{prop:upper}.
Homogeneity restores the factor $S^3$.

In dimension three, retain $S$ without normalization and put
$p_2=\operatorname{tr}(G^2)$, $p_3=\operatorname{tr}(G^3)$.
Form the algebraic curvature tensor given by the right-hand side of
the Gauss equation. Its Ricci contraction is $2I-G$. In a Gram
eigenframe, the three-dimensional Ricci decomposition gives
\[
 K_{ij}=1+g_k-S/2,\qquad\{i,j,k\}=\{1,2,3\}.
\]
The quadratic part of the Gauss tensor has components
\[
 \sum_a(\sigma_{jka}\sigma_{ila}-\sigma_{ika}\sigma_{jla})
 =-[A_i,A_j]_{kl}.
\]
In dimension three, this tensor is diagonal on two-forms in a Ricci
eigenbasis. Each sectional component occurs four times in its
ordered-index squared norm, so
\[
 Q=p_2+4\sum_k(g_k-S/2)^2=5p_2-S^2.
\]
Removing the constant-curvature term in \eqref{eq:2.4} also gives
\[
 \frac12\sum_a|[G,A_a]|^2+|V|^2
 =-\sum_{i<j}(g_k-S/2)(g_i-g_j)^2
 =3p_3-\frac12SQ.
\]
The last equality follows by expanding
\[
 \sum_{i<j}(g_i-g_j)^2=3p_2-S^2,
 \qquad
 \sum_{i<j}g_k(g_i-g_j)^2=4Sp_2-3p_3-S^3.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \mathcal B_t=\left(\frac{17}{5}-5t\right)Sp_2-3p_3
       +\left(\frac{11}{5}t-\frac45\right)S^3.
\]
The characteristic-polynomial identity gives
\[
 9\det\left(\frac35Sg-G\right)
 =\frac95Sp_2-3p_3-12\left(\frac S5\right)^3.
\]
Matching the $Sp_2$ coefficient selects $t=8/25$, and the $S^3$
coefficient then agrees. This proves \eqref{eq:2.9}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:gram} makes $(3S/5)g-G$ positive semidefinite,
so its determinant is nonnegative.

The estimates also prove the equality statement. For $n\ge4$ and
$\ell<\alpha$, the lower-range bound is strictly positive.
On the intermediate range, $b_0\ge(\alpha-\ell)(1-\ell)/2>0$,
$b_1>0$ and $b_2>0$ make the Bernstein quadratic strictly positive.
For $n=5,6$, the same lower bound for $b_0$, together with $M_0>0$,
gives strict positivity on the upper range; for $n\ge7$ it follows
from the positive Gram-deficit term in Proposition~\ref{prop:upper}.
Thus $S>0$ and $\mathcal B_t=0$ imply $\lambda_{\max}(G)=\alpha S$.
For $n=3$, zero determinant of the positive semidefinite tensor
$(3S/5)g-G$ gives the same conclusion.
head: environment

label: lem:axis
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:6.2
title: Proof
body_md:
At a point choose an orthonormal frame with $e_1=e$, and set
$h_{\beta l}=\langle\nabla_{e_l}e,e_\beta\rangle$ for $\beta>1$.
Since $e$ has unit length, differentiating \eqref{eq:6.1} gives
\begin{equation}\tag{6.2}\label{eq:6.2}
 T_{111l}=0,\qquad
 T_{11\beta l}=\frac{n+1}{\sqrt n}h_{\beta l},\qquad
 T_{1\beta\gamma l}=0,
 \quad T_{ijkl}=\sigma_{ijk;l}.
\end{equation}
Complete symmetry implies
$T_{11\beta1}=T_{111\beta}=0$ and
$T_{11\beta\gamma}=T_{1\beta\gamma1}=0$.
Thus every $h_{\beta l}$ vanishes, giving $\nabla e=0$.
Formula~\eqref{eq:6.1} then gives $\nabla\sigma=0$.
head: environment

label: eq:6.3
title: Proof
body_md:
Choose $t=8/25$ for $n=3$ and $t=\tau_n$ for $n\ge4$; in either
case $t\ge\tau_n$. Lemma~\ref{lem:derivative},
Proposition~\ref{prop:sextic}, and \eqref{eq:2.8} make all three
terms in \eqref{eq:2.7} nonnegative. Their integrals vanish, so each
term vanishes pointwise. In particular,
\[
 (1-S/c_n)S^2=0.
\]
Connectedness gives $S\equiv0$ or $S\equivc_n$.

If $S=0$, the ambient Gauss formula shows that the real span of $F$
and $dF(TM)$ is a fixed $(n+1)$-plane. This plane is Lagrangian by
the Legendrian condition. The immersion into its great sphere is a
local isometry; compactness makes it a surjective covering, and simple
connectedness of $\mathbb S^n$ makes the covering one-sheeted. A unitary
transformation sends the plane to the standard real subspace.

Suppose henceforth that $S=c_n$. We also have $\mathcal B_t=0$.
The equality implication in Proposition~\ref{prop:sextic} gives
$\lambda_{\max}(G)=\alpha S$. Lemma~\ref{lem:gram} determines
the cubic, with independent components
\[
 \sigma_{111}=\frac{n-1}{\sqrt n},\qquad
 \sigma_{1\beta\gamma}=-\frac{\delta_{\beta\gamma}}{\sqrt n},
 \qquad \sigma_{11\beta}=\sigma_{\beta\gamma\delta}=0,
\]
after orienting its axis. In particular,
\[
 G=\operatorname{diag}(n-1,2/n,\ldots,2/n),\qquad
 V=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)(n+1)}{n\sqrt n}\,e^\flat.
\]
Since $n\ge3$, the one-form $V$ is nowhere zero, so
$e=V^\sharp/|V|$ defines a smooth global axis. Its cubic is exactly
\eqref{eq:6.1}. Lemma~\ref{lem:axis} now gives $\nabla e=0$ and
$\nabla\sigma=0$.

We identify tangent vectors with their images under $dF$. For $X\perp e$,
the ambient Gauss formula gives
\begin{equation}\tag{6.3}\label{eq:6.3}
 \begin{aligned}
 D_Ze&=-\frac1{\sqrt n}JZ+\sqrt n\,\xi(Z)Je-\xi(Z)F,\\
 D_ZX&=\nabla_ZX-
       \frac{\xi(Z)JX+\langle Z,X\rangle Je}{\sqrt n}
       -\langle Z,X\rangle F.
 \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
On the universal cover, the parallel one-form $\xi$ is exact; write
$\mathrm d t=\xi$. Define
\begin{equation}\tag{6.4}\label{eq:6.4}
 q=e^{-i\sqrt n t}\frac{F-\sqrt n\,Je}{\sqrt{n+1}},\qquad
 \psi=e^{it/\sqrt n}\frac{\sqrt n F+Je}{\sqrt{n+1}}.
\end{equation}
For example,
$D_Z(F-\sqrt n\,Je)=i\sqrt n\,\xi(Z)(F-\sqrt n\,Je)$.
Differentiating both expressions therefore yields
\begin{equation}\tag{6.5}\label{eq:6.5}
 Dq=0,\qquad
 \mathrm d\psi(Z)=\sqrt{\frac{n+1}{n}}\,e^{it/\sqrt n}
             (Z-\xi(Z)e).
\end{equation}
For $X\perp e$, a second differentiation gives
\begin{equation}\tag{6.6}\label{eq:6.6}
 D_Z(\mathrm d\psi(X))
 =\mathrm d\psi(\nabla_ZX)-\frac{n+1}{n}\langle Z,X\rangle\psi.
\end{equation}
Indeed, the phase derivative cancels the term
$-\xi(Z)JX/\sqrt n$ in \eqref{eq:6.3}; the remaining normal terms
combine into a multiple of $\sqrt n F+Je$. These identities hold
for arbitrary $Z$.

Before multiplication by their phase factors, both
$F-\sqrt n\,Je$ and $\sqrt n F+Je$ have squared norm $n+1$.
The real and imaginary parts of their Hermitian inner product vanish, using
$\langle F,Je\rangle=\langle JF,e\rangle=0$.
Their Hermitian products with a transverse vector $X$ vanish as well.
Multiplication by complex phases preserves these zero products.
Thus $q$ and $\psi$ are unit vectors, and $q$ is Hermitian orthogonal
to $\psi$ and $\mathrm d\psi(TM)$.

By \eqref{eq:6.5}--\eqref{eq:6.6}, ambient derivatives of local fields spanning
$\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{\psi,\mathrm d\psi(e^\perp)\}$ remain in this
span. It therefore defines a fixed real $n$-plane on the connected
universal cover. The Legendrian condition gives
\[
 \langle J\psi,\mathrm d\psi(X)\rangle=0,\qquad
 \langle J\mathrm d\psi(X),\mathrm d\psi(Y)\rangle=0
 \quad(X,Y\perp e).
\]
Hence this real plane is Lagrangian in the complex orthogonal
complement of $q$. A fixed unitary transformation sends $q$ to the
first coordinate vector and the plane to $\mathbb R^n\subset\mathbb C^n$.
After this transformation, we identify $\psi$ with its last $n$
coordinates, so that $\psi$ takes values in
$\mathbb S^{n-1}\subset\mathbb R^n$. Let $\widetilde F$ denote the lift of $F$ to
the universal cover. Solving \eqref{eq:6.4} gives
\[
 \widetilde F(p)=\left(
 \frac{e^{i\sqrt n\,t(p)}}{\sqrt{n+1}},
 \sqrt{\frac n{n+1}}e^{-it(p)/\sqrt n}\psi(p)\right).
\]
Hence the lifted immersion has image in \eqref{eq:1.1}, with parameters
$\theta=t(p)/\sqrt n$ and $x=\psi(p)$.

We determine the global identifications of the model. Its induced
metric is
\[
 n\,\mathrm d\theta^2+\frac n{n+1}g_{\mathbb S^{n-1}},
\]
so it is an immersion. Two parameters $(\theta,x)$ and $(\varphi,y)$
have the same image exactly when
\[
 e^{in(\varphi-\theta)}=1,\qquad
 y=e^{i(\varphi-\theta)}x.
\]
Since $x,y$ are real unit vectors, $\varphi-\theta\in\pi\mathbb Z$.
Modulo $2\pi$, the only extra identification is
$(\theta,x)\sim(\theta+\pi,-x)$ for even $n$.
The map on the stated compact quotient is injective, hence an
embedding. Call its connected image $C_n$. The original immersion
has image in $C_n$ and is a local diffeomorphism onto it. Its image
is open and, by compactness, closed, so it equals $C_n$.
A proper local diffeomorphism is a covering, and compactness makes
the covering finite.

Finally, the model is minimal Legendrian and attains the pinching value. For \eqref{eq:1.1}, take
$e=F_\theta/\sqrt n$ and unit transverse vectors
$e_\beta=(0,e^{-i\theta}v_\beta)$, where the $v_\beta$ are
orthonormal tangent vectors to $\mathbb S^{n-1}$. The contact form vanishes:
\[
 \langle JF,F_\theta\rangle=\frac n{n+1}-\frac n{n+1}=0,
 \qquad \langle JF,\mathrm d F(v)\rangle=0.
\]
Differentiation gives
\[
 \langle D_ee,Je\rangle=\frac{n-1}{\sqrt n},\qquad
 \langle D_ee_\beta,Je_\gamma\rangle
 =-\frac{\delta_{\beta\gamma}}{\sqrt n},
\]
while $\sigma_{11\beta}$ and $\sigma_{\beta\gamma\delta}$ vanish.
By symmetry, equivalently,
\[
 B(e,e)=\frac{n-1}{\sqrt n}Je,\qquad
 B(e,e_\beta)=-\frac1{\sqrt n}Je_\beta,\qquad
 B(e_\beta,e_\gamma)=-\frac{\delta_{\beta\gamma}}{\sqrt n}Je.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \operatorname{tr} B=0,\qquad
 |B|^2=\frac{(n-1)^2+3(n-1)}n=c_n.
\]
head: environment
